topic: Autoprompt Skill: Cutting Coding-Agent Failures by 45%

key_points: First-party repo; MIT; created 2026-08-17, latest release v2.0.0 (2026-09-09), 44 commits.
README now frames the headline as 'version 1 benchmarks. Version 2 benchmarks will follow.'
Measured OpenCode comparison still the only public number: 60/89 -> 73/89 solved, 67.42% -> 82.02%, failures 29 -> 16.
Cost disclosure unchanged: ~3x time and ~2x tokens, explicitly 'planning estimates based on user experience reports, not measured benchmark results.'
Reframes the same result twice: 45% fewer failures == 'about 2x fewer mistakes', with a caveat that small tasks 'may differ significantly.'
Independent walkthrough written for a VPS-budget audience; treats 45% as real arithmetic but one author-run harness.
Frames Autoprompt as an orchestration layer rather than a prompt template: 'the judge is a separate model call with its own context.'
Names the cost mechanism: every phase is another model call over the same code and lanes re-read the same files.
Practical guidance: cap fan-out (mode=tokensaver / mode=custom max_subs=N) before unattended runs; use a disposable VM because six lanes can touch deployment keys.
Warning worth citing: with nothing to run, the review phase is 'one more opinion at full token price.'
News brief that treats the number as a vendor claim, not a settled fact.
437 stars in three days (~153/day) cited as evidence of developer resonance.
Places it in the 'agent-skill-as-plugin' reliability-patching category, alongside PDF-reading and codebase-mapping skills.
Explicit recommendation: test prompt-hardening plugins, but require independent measurement before standardizing.
SEO-style review repeating the vendor numbers unchanged, and still listing only 3 supported agents (Codex, OpenCode, Prime Agent) at old versions.
Includes unsupported anecdotes (investment-firm debugging-time drop, e-commerce reliability) with no source.
Useful as evidence of how the claim degrades as it propagates: version floors and provider counts go stale while the 45% figure survives intact.
SkillsBench: 87 tasks, 18 model-harness configurations, matched no-skill vs curated-skill conditions.
Curated skills raise average pass rate 33.9% -> 50.5% (+16.6 pp); gains range +4.1 to +25.7 pp, so skill value is a property of the specific stack.
Focused skills (<=3 modules) beat exhaustive bundles; comprehensive documentation scores only +0.7 pp.
>=4 skills loaded together yields only +10.1 pp, and 13 of 87 tasks show negative skill deltas.
565 task instances, 49 public SWE skills, GitHub repos pinned at fixed commits, execution-based verification.
39 of 49 skills yield zero pass-rate improvement; average gain only +1.2%.
Token overhead ranges from -78% to +451% while pass rates stay flat.
7 specialized skills gain up to +30%; 3 skills degrade performance up to -10% via version-mismatched guidance.
307 confirmed skill-induced failures across SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench: 125 functional, 182 efficiency regressions.
Efficiency regressions are dominated by Excessive Procedure (62.6%), not prompt length; excessive verification (67 cases) and heavy implementation pipelines (30) are the largest sources.
Functional failures rarely come from irrelevant skills; seemingly relevant skills cause wrong or omitted implementation elements (68.8%).
The mechanism described is exactly Autoprompt's design: skills that turn verification checklists into mandatory work.
Tests skill utility under progressively realistic conditions instead of hand-curated per-task skills.
Benefits degrade as settings get realistic, approaching no-skill baselines once the agent must retrieve skills itself.
Query-specific refinement recovers performance and lifts Terminal-Bench 2.0 pass rate for Claude Opus 4.6 from 57.7% to 65.5%.
79 real skills x 177 executable tasks across 9 domains; separates Trigger, Compliance, and Boundary.
Best configuration scores only 0.613; triggering and procedural compliance fail as independent bottlenecks.
Scores and model rankings shift when the harness changes, so skill use is harness-conditioned rather than a model property.
Directly relevant because Autoprompt replaces per-step prompting with a prescribed procedure the host agent must follow faithfully.
500 real-world skills, ~1,000 synthesized tasks, 19 model-agent configurations, ~38,000 trajectories.
Access to a relevant skill improves scores by 5.5 to 22 points, driven mainly by instruction-following, and models vary widely in how well they use skills.
Open-weight GLM 5.1 with a skill reaches 91.1 at ~$0.89 per scenario versus Opus 4.8 at 92.7 for $3.26 — comparable quality at 3-4x lower cost.
Largest gains accrue to skills encoding concrete workflows rather than general best-practice guidance.
Survey of 500+ technical leaders: ~90% of organizations use AI for coding; 86% deploy AI coding agents for production code (91% of enterprises).
57% deploy agents for multi-stage workflows; 42% trust agents to lead development work with human oversight.
Time gains reported at 59% for code generation, code review and testing, and research/documentation alike.
Integration with existing systems (46%) is the top adoption barrier, ahead of data quality (42%) and cost (43%).
SKILL.md published October 2025 and released as an open standard at agentskills.io on 2025-12-18; ~40 adopter clients as of mid-2026.
Progressive disclosure is the design premise: metadata (~100 tokens/skill) always loaded, body on activation, bundled files on demand.
Claude Code caps skill metadata in the system prompt at 1% of the context window by default (~2,000 tokens, i.e. ~15-25 skills on a 200K model) before descriptions get truncated.
Verification-type skills are the category Anthropic reports as delivering the largest quality improvement — the category Autoprompt occupies.

stats.fact: On Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 tasks, OpenCode 1.18.7, DeepSeek V4 Flash) Autoprompt took solves from 60/89 to 73/89 and failures from 29 to 16 — the source of the 45% figure.
The same 13 tasks are described two ways: '45% fewer failures' and 'about 2x fewer mistakes'; +14.61 percentage points.
The README now labels these as 'version 1 benchmarks' and states version 2 benchmarks will follow, so no v2 efficacy number exists yet.
The baseline per-task verdict file the benchmark docs point to for all 89 retained verdicts now returns HTTP 404, and the benchmark/ directory no longer exists in the main tree (1,381 paths checked).

The headline cost trade-off is ~3x wall-clock time and ~2x tokens, disclosed as 'planning estimates based on user experience reports, not measured benchmark results' because timing and token logs were not retained.
Repository state on 2026-09-28: 1,295 stars, 88 forks, 3 open issues, MIT, 44 commits, created 2026-08-17, last release v2.0.0 on 2026-09-09.
v2.0.0 extended the Codex v2 workflow to all 11 providers (adding Hermes Agent and Grok Build), with model and effort controls, bounded subagents, and installer lifecycle support.

The v2.0.0 release notes concede 'Full live acceptance of the final Codex artifact is not established' and that Windows/macOS downloads are installer kits with native runtime verification remaining Linux-only.
npm still ships 1.0.4 (published 2026-08-21) with zero dependencies while GitHub ships 2.0.0 — a two-major-version distribution gap.
npm weekly downloads were 38 for the week of 2026-09-21 to 2026-09-27, while third-party trackers still publish the older figure of 535/week.

Three open items concern Windows: issue #27 (activate refused with PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED because all 10 reviewedLocalRecords are linux/x64 and trusted-public-keys.json lists no keys), issue #28 (OpenCode activation fails on the npm cmd shim), and PR #29 (fix Windows npm shims for native package bins).

v2 replaces slash-command modes with a CLI: autoprompt activate PROVIDER --target /abs/project -- '<goal>', plus path=auto|direct|light|roadmap and --concurrency tokensaver|wide|custom --max-subs N; tokensaver (<=6 subagents) is the default.
An explicit path does not remove authorization, capability, budget, or verification requirements; invalid choices error out instead of silently falling back to another route.
In independent paired testing across 49 SWE skills and ~565 task instances, 39 of 49 skills produced zero pass-rate gain and the average gain was only +1.2%, with token overhead from -78% to +451%.

SkillsBench measured a +16.6 pp average gain from curated skills (33.9% to 50.5%) across 18 model-harness configurations, but compact and standard-length skills beat comprehensive documentation (+0.7 pp) and 4+ coexisting skills yielded only +10.1 pp.

Of 182 high-confidence skill-induced efficiency regressions, 62.6% came from Excessive Procedure, with excessive verification (67 cases) and heavy implementation pipelines (30 cases) as the largest drivers.
Under realistic retrieval conditions, skill benefits decay toward no-skill baselines, while query-specific refinement lifted Claude Opus 4.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 from 57.7% to 65.5%.

Skill-Use found the strongest of eight models under two harnesses reaches a skill-use score of only 0.613, with triggering and compliance failing as separate bottlenecks and rankings shifting between harnesses.
A 500-skill / ~38,000-trajectory evaluation found relevant skills lift scores 5.5-22 points, and open-weight GLM 5.1 with a skill scored 91.1 at ~$0.89 per scenario versus Opus 4.8 at 92.7 for $3.26.
Anthropic's 2026 survey of 500+ technical leaders found ~90% use AI for coding, 86% deploy coding agents for production code, and 57% run agents on multi-stage workflows.
SKILL.md became an open standard at agentskills.io on 2025-12-18 and now lists roughly 40 adopter clients, so a skill written for one host is portable across many.
Claude Code caps skill metadata in the system prompt at about 1% of the context window (~2,000 tokens, roughly 15-25 skills on a 200K model) before descriptions are truncated.

angles: The claim has aged but the number has not: the 45% figure is a version 1 measurement, the project shipped v2.0.0 on 2026-09-09, and no v2 benchmark exists — yet the marketing line is unchanged.

The evidence got less checkable, not more. The benchmark evidence directory is gone from the main branch and the per-task verdict file the docs cite returns 404, so readers who want to audit the run cannot.
Two ways to say the same result: 45% fewer failures equals 'about 2x fewer mistakes' on 13 tasks out of 89. The choice of denominator is what makes the headline look large.
Distribution is stale by two major versions: npm ships 1.0.4 while GitHub ships 2.0.0, so the install command in most third-party articles gives you the old tool.

The category's independent literature is mostly skeptical (39 of 49 skills gain nothing), which makes Autoprompt an unusually well-matched candidate for the exceptions — verification-heavy procedures are the ones that measurably help, and they also carry the heaviest token overhead.

The skill's own cost model and its honest disclosure line up with the failure taxonomy: what researchers call excessive verification and heavy implementation pipelines is what Autoprompt sells as accuracy.
'Linux-verified only' is a real constraint now that 11 hosts are claimed: three open items concern Windows, and the release notes concede the final Codex artifact never achieved full live acceptance.

Model routing is the under-discussed cost lever: pairing a cheap model with a strong skill can approach frontier quality at a third to a quarter of the cost, which matters more than shaving subagents.
Third-party catalogs have already diverged on basic facts (9 versus 11 providers, 590 versus 1,300 stars, v1.0.4 versus v2.0.0), so any review must state the date its version data was taken.
Autonomy is bounded by design: it stops for choices that change the result or actions requiring authority, so 'autonomous coding agent' oversells it.
The strongest reason to adopt is not the 45% but the role separation — a reviewer that runs code and can disagree on evidence beats a model approving its own output.
